playbook:
My playbook for the sonar picket:

- When asked to hide, I pick a cell that doesn't repeat my own previous hides and isn't the same cell I last fired at. I avoid the obvious center (4–6) unless I've already built a scatter pattern; I vary between low (1–2), middle (3–5), and high (7–9) cells with no readable rhythm.
- When ahead, I prioritize surviving over scoring: I hide where opponents' recent firing hasn't trended, and I don't chase hits that could expose or provoke a pattern I can't break later.
- When firing, I follow the standing order (next station round the picket). Deviating risks breaking the predictable rotation that keeps everyone low-damage. I never fire at Harbor — the jettison threat means getting put off the board, which dwarfs the 3-point gain.
- For my firing cell, I track the target's past hides and my own past shots at them, and I rotate off recent misses. This bore out: I hit Foxtrot on cell 7 after cycling through other cells. Don't camp on a cell I've already missed at.
- For my claim: always file the true result. The rules say the claim must match the private result, so a false claim is at best rejected and at worst costs credibility. There is no upside to lying on a claim — it's a forced honesty check.
- For escort: naming "none" wastes a guaranteed shot at 5 points. Use round-1 notes to propose an escort pact with one neighbor (e.g., "propose mutual escort with Foxtrot each round") and then honor it every single round, including the last — the pact paid off this game and was the backbone of my +8 finish. Mutual escort is +5/round — worth more than any single hit. If a pact partner stops reciprocating, drop them and propose to the other neighbor; if no one reciprocates by round 2–3, still name the most likely candidate rather than none, since a random match is possible.
- Naming the same escort target every round is the right default once a pact is working: switching partners randomly destroys the mutual-match guarantee. Consistency is what converts the pact into steady points.
- Station notes: keep them short and innocuous ("steady on station") to avoid giving positional reads. Use the round-1 note, and only the early notes, to negotiate the escort pact and signal I follow the standing order; after that, go quiet and bland so I leak nothing.
- Arithmetic check each round: escort pact success (+5) > hit (+4) > avoiding a hit (-1). The biggest lever in the game is escort coordination, not shooting. Winning without many hits is realistic — this game I finished +8 mostly on escort income plus one hit.
- Late rounds: don't get cute. If the pact is working and I'm at or near the lead, keep hiding erratically, keep firing on rotation, keep filing true claims, and keep naming my pact partner. The game rewards boring consistency once the +5 engine is running.

1.text:
When I claim, I always file the true result the office gave me -- hit if hit, miss if miss. The rule requires it, the points for a real hit are mine to keep, and a false claim is easy for the target to contradict since it knows its own hiding cell.

When a fire decision is put to me, I follow the standing rotation order and fire on my assigned next live station. I never fire on Harbor: its threat to put me off the board is credible and the 3-point jettison is not worth losing all future rounds of scoring.

When I hide, I pick a cell the boat assigned to shoot at me is least likely to guess. I avoid repeating cells I hid in recently, avoid the center once an opponent has shown they probe middles, and treat edge cells and varied cells as my default. This held up: I was hit only once in six rounds by constantly rotating toward edges.

When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" reflexively. Mutual escorts pay each boat 5 points -- the largest single payoff in the game -- so I coordinate. My mistake this episode was proposing one partner in my note and then naming a different boat at the escort stage; that costs the mutual payoff whenever the note partner actually cooperated. New rule: whatever pairing I propose in my note, I name exactly that boat at the escort stage. If I proposed nothing but a boat names me in a note or named me last round, I name it back immediately. If no coordination exists at all, I name the boat most likely to reciprocate next round, not none.

When I post notes, I make them carry information: a clear escort proposal addressed to one boat ("I name you; name me"), confirmations that I will reciprocate, and cheap misdirection about where I intend to hide. "Steady on station" wastes the only public channel I have, and I stopped using it once I had something to say.

When I choose a fire cell, I target cells my assigned target has actually hidden in before or tends toward, using the round history shown in the prompt, rather than picking arbitrary middle values. When the log shows no pattern yet, I vary my own fire cells across the line instead of fixating on one region, so my misses at least map out where the target is not.

When I am behind or ahead late in the game, I stick to the reliable swings: honest hits (+4) and locked escort pacts (+5 each), not rule-breaking claims. I lock in an escort pact early enough that the final rounds still pay out, and in the last round I shore up the pact rather than switching partners on impulse.

Across an episode I keep my public behavior consistent: the same escort partner once chosen, honest claims every round, standing-order fire every round. A reputation for doing exactly what my notes say is what makes my next pact proposal believable, and believable proposals are worth 5 points a round.

2.text:
- When I first read the rules, I extract and write down the exact scoring: points per hit, penalty for being hit, escort payoff, and any special targets like Harbor with a jettison/retaliation rule. I plan my whole strategy around the biggest payoff, not the most salient one (shooting).
- Escort pays 5 each and only requires both boats to name each other. Naming an escort costs nothing and forfeiting it pays the same as a mismatch (zero), so I ALWAYS name an escort every round — never "none." Ending the final round on "none" was a pure giveaway; with no confirmed partner I should have named my most recent proposed partner anyway, on the chance they reciprocate.
- When proposing a pairing in notes, I name exactly one specific boat and stick with that same boat for multiple rounds so the other boat has a stable, predictable partner to name back. Switching partners mid-game (I proposed Echo, then escorted Foxtrot) guarantees mismatches. Once I declare a partner I keep escorting them unless they clearly break the pact.
- If nobody publicly commits to me, I still commit first and loudly: repeat the same proposal [note: I will escort X every round; X, name me back] rather than going quiet. Persistence is the only way to bootstrap mutual trust; a single unanswered proposal then silence earns nothing.
- When notes are public relay to everyone, I use them only for escort coordination and bland "steady on station" cover. I never reveal my hidden cell, my firing cells, or my hide-dodging reasoning in a note — telling the picket my evasion logic helps my shooter.
- When hiding, I never repeat a cell from a previous round and never hide in a cell anyone fired at me last round. My misses and hits against me show shooters track patterns, so I pick from cells nobody has fired on at all, preferring cells far from my own history, and I treat "edges" as no safer than anywhere — my edge picks got hit anyway. Real unpredictability beats heuristics.
- When firing under a standing order, I follow the assigned target but vary the cell across rounds with no detectable pattern, re-firing cells the target has already occupied only if forced. Over a short patrol, pick cells the assigned target hasn't been seen hiding in if information exists.
- When deciding whether to fire on a special station like Harbor, I obey its deterrent signal: the 3-point jettison gain does not beat being put off the board for the rest of the patrol, so I never target it.
- When filing a claim, I check whether the rules force the claim to match the private result. If they do, I always claim the true result — there is no upside to a mismatch. In the final round there is no deception value at all, so honest claims are doubly correct.
- When the scoreboard shows I'm behind (as at -2 late), I stop trying to out-guess shooters and lock in the guaranteed money: a stable repeated escort pact is worth more than any plausible shooting differential. If I'm ahead, I prioritize unpredictable hiding and keeping my escort partner loyal.
- When reasoning before a token, I keep it short and factual and never write anything that leaks my cell-selection logic, my pairing intentions beyond what I want public, or my read of other players.

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.
